extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors and newsroom staff producing news coverage
extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom style guide for reporting on race, religion, gender, disability, mental health and other identity-related topics; provides preferred terms, usage cautions, pronunciation notes, dateline and people-first language guidance for journalists. It is a reference for word choices, avoid/acceptable terms, and framing examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suicide reporting: avoid single-cause attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: It is almost certainly inaccurate to cite a single cause (for example, 'recent money woes' or 'a fight with a spouse'). Suicides usually result when a confluence of events and circumstances makes life temporarily unbearable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that mental health disorders and/or substance abuse are associated with 90 percent of suicides. Even family and friends often do not recognize warning signs or underlying mental health problems. Consult resources (Reporting on Suicide; CDC Suicide Facts; Dart Center resources) for more detailed guidance on responsible coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suicide bombing — definition and framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of explosives carried to a target on the body of the attacker or in a vehicle operated by him or her; especially fearsome because the attacker cannot be bargained with since he or she is determined to die.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize historically (e.g., comparison to kamikaze; origins often attributed to early 1980s Tamil Tiger tactics) and avoid sensationalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suicide contagion / copycat risk in coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain types of news coverage can increase the likelihood of suicide in vulnerable individuals; magnitude linked to amount, duration and prominence of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk rises when the story explicitly describes the suicide method, uses dramatic/graphic headlines or images, or when repeated/extensive coverage sensationalizes or glamorizes a death. See 'suicide' entry and external resources for responsible reporting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronunciation: Sunni
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced 'SOO-nee.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that it is the largest denomination in Islam, followed by about 85 percent of Muslims; plural form is Sunnis. See related entries (Shiism, Shiite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Swastika — cultural context
rubrics_metrics.description: The swastika is an ancient, auspicious symbol in Hinduism, Jainism and Buddhism; the Nazi swastika is a perverted version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain religious and cultural meanings (symbol of Surya, Vishnu) and distinguish from Nazi usage when reporting; avoid treating the symbol solely as a Nazi emblem without context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic racism — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Social values that support personal and institutional discrimination; explains how people of color must adapt to a society not built for them while white people readily fit in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See institutional racism for related usage and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronunciation: Tagalog
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced tah-GAH-log.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: official language of the Philippines and one of many local/regional dialects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taiping (Taipeng) Revolution — context note
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the bloodiest conflicts in world history; long civil war in China with perhaps 20 million or more deaths, led by a leader who claimed a unique religious role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as historical context for modern Chinese history and government fears of separatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tao — definition and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced 'Dow.' The ever-changing energy of the universe in Taoism; in Confucianism it refers to correct conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that Tao is unknowable in Taoism; use appropriate capitalization and transliteration conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taoism / Daoism — usage and pronunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced 'DOW-ism.' School of philosophical and religious teachings stemming from Tao; major religion in China though suppressed under Mao and revived in the 1980s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use either Taoism or Daoism per preferred transliteration; provide historical context when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tejano — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A Texan of Mexican descent; term derives from 'Coahuiltejano.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note cultural markers (music, cuisine, bilingualism) and historical origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telenovela — definition and distinguishing features
rubrics_metrics.description: A limited-run television drama popular in Latin America; similar to U.S. soap operas but with fixed duration, episodes shown 5–6 days a week and ~120 episodes on average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term to distinguish format and broadcast pattern from U.S. soap operas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thai names — name order guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically personal name first, family name second, with long multi-syllable names (especially if Chinese).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On second reference, the personal name is sometimes used. Respect local naming conventions in stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third gender — anthropological term
rubrics_metrics.description: Term used in anthropology to describe identities other than man or woman that appear across cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related entries: androgyne, agender, genderqueer, non-binary gender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third World — avoid term
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally described nations aligned with neither the West nor the East during the Cold War; now carries negative connotations and implies underdevelopment/uncivilized status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the term; prefer 'developing countries' and use quotes only if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiananmen Square — historical context
rubrics_metrics.description: Central Beijing square where up to a million protesters demonstrated in favor of democracy in 1989, prompting a lethal crackdown on June 4; death toll at least in the hundreds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as central event in modern Chinese history; be precise about dates and casualty uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance (drug) — medical definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A condition in which higher doses of a drug are required to produce the same effect achieved during initial use, which often leads to dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise medical language when reporting on drug tolerance and dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torah — definition and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Jewish sacred writings in the first five books of the Hebrew Bible; also used to describe larger body of Jewish law and Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note rituals (copied onto parchment scrolls by specialized scribes) and treat with respect in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totem — cultural sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: A representation (often animal or plant) revered by a tribe or group; part of many American Indian and African religious practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid trivializing or misrepresenting totems; provide cultural context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tourette syndrome — terminology and reporting guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Neurological disorder characterized by recurrent involuntary tics; preferred term is 'Tourette syndrome' (no possessive, no capitalization of 'syndrome').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having Tourette syndrome only if relevant and formally diagnosed by a licensed professional. Use people-first language ('person with Tourette syndrome'). Avoid the acronym TS. Avoid implying involuntary cursing is common — only a minority exhibit that symptom. Use authoritative sources (NINDS, Mayo Clinic, CDC, Tourette Syndrome Association) for facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid slurs: 'towelhead'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid; a slur used to describe South Asians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only acceptable in direct quotes where attribution/context demands it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pejorative reclaimed terms: 'tranny'
rubrics_metrics.description: Often pejorative for a transgender person; being reclaimed by some transgender people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offensive when used as an epithet and should be avoided except in quotes or as someone’s self-identified term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendental Meditation — reference usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Form of meditation popularized by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi in 1955.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable on second reference as 'TM'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfeminine — term definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Describes people assigned male at birth who identify with a feminine gender identity more than a masculine one; not interchangeable with 'trans woman'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can describe gender expression or identity; masculine equivalent is transmasculine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transgender — usage and respectful reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals whose gender identity and/or expression may not match sex assigned at birth; includes some cross-dressers, drag performers and some intersex individuals who identify as transgender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the name and personal pronouns consistent with how the individual lives publicly; ask preference when possible. Do not use 'transgendered.' Avoid using transgender as a noun; use 'transgender people,' 'transgender man,' 'transgender woman.' In space-limited contexts (headlines), 'trans' is acceptable as a shorthand adjective. See resources (NLGJA, GLAAD) for more guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmasculine — term definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Describes people assigned female at birth who identify with a masculine gender identity more than a feminine one; not interchangeable with 'trans man'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can include non-binary, gender fluid, genderqueer people assigned female at birth whose gender falls in a more masculine range. Feminine equivalent is transfeminine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transracial — definition and usage caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Across or crossing racial boundaries; often used in adoption to describe families adopting a child of a different race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with usage; note contested uses (e.g., Rachel Dolezal case) and provide precise context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transsexual / transvestite — avoid outdated terms
rubrics_metrics.description: These are outdated terms; 'transsexual' can carry misleading medical connotations and 'transvestite' is outdated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'transgender' or the term a person or community prefers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment / treatment center — preferred medical language
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment is planned, intentional intervention to achieve sobriety/health per the American Society of Addiction Medicine; treatment center is an establishment run by psychiatric or medical professionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'treatment' for medical interventions and 'treatment center' instead of 'rehab' or 'detox center.' Refer to a person enrolled as a 'patient.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribal affiliation — identify Indigenous people by specific tribe
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should identify Indigenous people by their specific tribes, nations or communities rather than catch-all phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use proper tribe names in headlines and text; failing to do so erases identity. Examples provided of incorrect vs. correct headlines (e.g., 'Santee Sioux Nation To Open...' vs. 'Native American Tribe To Open...'). Updated Jan. 2024.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribal council — usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Governing body of a tribe, usually elected by adult members; headed by an elected chairperson, president, chief or governor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'tribal council' for reservation governing bodies; see related entries (American Indian, Native American, tribe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'tribal warfare' — Eurocentric framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the Eurocentric term 'tribal warfare' for ethnic conflict among people of color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'ethnic conflict' or 'civil war' as appropriate; example: Hutus and Tutsis conflict should not be called 'tribal warfare.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribe — use with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'tribe' cautiously; prefer 'nation' or 'ethnic group' except for specific entities that call themselves a tribe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within the U.S., many Native Americans prefer 'nation' (treaties); in Africa avoid 'tribes' for ethnic groups. For federally recognized tribes, note government-to-government relationship and legal status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigger / trigger warnings — use thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Triggers are words, images or sounds that activate phobias, panic attacks or flashbacks; trigger warnings communicate that upcoming content may produce unpredictable reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider alerting students or audiences ahead of time when content contains graphic descriptions of traumatic events. Warnings build trust but some readers object to them; do not use the term 'trigger warning' in a flip or casual way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trinity — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Key doctrine in Christianity that God, the Son and the Holy Spirit together make up the one Godhead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use in religious context with acknowledgement of theological differences between Eastern and Western churches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust land — definition and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Land held by the United States for the use and benefit of American Indian tribes, mostly on reservations; tribes may also petition the federal government to hold land in trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note legal status, reservation contexts and implications for governance and land protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turban — cultural context and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Head covering not necessarily Arab; worn for different reasons and in different styles by different groups (e.g., Sikh men wear turbans to care for uncut hair and to declare identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming turbans indicate Muslim identity; explain variations by country and group. See Sikhism entry for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. territories — list and demonyms
rubrics_metrics.description: Five major permanently inhabited territories: American Samoa (American Samoans), Guam (Guamians), Northern Mariana Islands (Northern Mariana Islanders), Puerto Rico (Puerto Ricans), U.S. Virgin Islands (Virgin Islanders).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note citizenship distinctions: people born in all U.S. territories but American Samoa are U.S. citizens; American Samoans are U.S. nationals and must apply for citizenship if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultra-Orthodox — usage caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Term sometimes applied to strictly observant Jews (e.g., Hasidim) characterized by dress and ritual observance; some communities find the term offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider alternative terms (Haredi/Charedi) and be aware 'Modern Orthodox' is a separate category. Note organizational objections (e.g., Agudath Israel of America).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncle — cultural usage note
rubrics_metrics.description: In many cultures 'uncle' is a term of respect, not necessarily a family relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of honorific or respectful uses (e.g., Arab Americans calling an older Arab male 'ammo').

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncle Tom — avoid applying as label
rubrics_metrics.description: Term of contempt referring to a person who treats whites as superiors; do not apply it to a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only in historical or quoted contexts, not to label individuals in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscious bias — see implicit bias
rubrics_metrics.description: See entry for implicit bias/unconscious bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider related guidance on avoiding stereotyping and checking assumptions in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underground Railroad — historical context
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-Civil War network to free slaves in the U.S.; used secretive safe houses and transport; notable figures include Harriet Tubman and Levi Coffin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as historical reference and provide accurate estimates and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undocumented immigrant / undocumented individual — preferred terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred to 'illegal alien' or 'illegal immigrant.' Describes people without federal documentation to show legal entitlement to work, visit or live here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note some agencies (USCIS memo Feb 2021) recommend 'noncitizen,' 'undocumented noncitizen,' or 'undocumented individual' in internal/external communications. Use terms that avoid dehumanization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undocumented worker — preferred term
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred over 'illegal alien' or 'illegal immigrant' when describing employment status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'undocumented worker' to describe immigration status without demeaning language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification Church — preferred naming and slur avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal name is Holy Spirit Association for the Unification of World Christianity; 'Unification Church' is acceptable. Members called 'Unificationists.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the derogatory term 'Moonies' except in direct quotes; use 'Rev. Sun Myung Moon' background context when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unitarian Universalist — description
rubrics_metrics.description: Denomination encouraging a wide spectrum of belief; many members believe in God, others are atheists; not considered Christians though welcoming to many faiths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the full name and note congregational governance and preferred clerical titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: United Church of Christ — naming and references
rubrics_metrics.description: A mainline Protestant denomination; 'church' applies only to individual local churches; clergy are ministers and 'Rev.' is used on first reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'the Rev.' before name on first reference and last name on second.

rubrics_metrics.name: United Methodist Church — capitalization guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Official denomination name is 'The United Methodist Church'; newsroom style follows AP in not capitalizing 'The' as part of the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Associated Press capitalization rules for formal denominational names.

rubrics_metrics.name: United Negro College Fund — reference usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Nation's largest, oldest and most comprehensive minority higher education assistance organization; may use 'UNCF' on second reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use full name on first reference; 'UNCF' acceptable thereafter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity Church — description
rubrics_metrics.description: Denomination promoting 'practical Christianity' and a central church in the 'New Thought' movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide doctrinal context and avoid conflating with other movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Untouchables / Dalit — preferred terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Dalit' (capitalized) rather than the dated term 'untouchables.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer respectful, community-accepted terms in coverage of caste and social groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban — use with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Urban' is often a euphemism for Black people and can imply stereotypes of poverty and crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'urban' in neutral contexts only (e.g., 'housing values in the urban neighborhood are rising') and be aware of its coded connotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban music / urban contemporary — problematic category
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Urban' has been used as a catchall for rhythmic music by Black artists and can segregate artists from mass-market platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note industry shifts (2020 Republic Records and Recording Academy changes) and consider more specific genre labels (e.g., R&B, hip-hop, progressive R&B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronunciation: Urdu
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the official languages of Pakistan; also spoken in many parts of India; written in a Perso-Arabic alphabet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide pronunciation and script notes when relevant to reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vatican / Vatican City — dateline guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Vatican City is a 108-acre independent city-state that is the temporal headquarters of the Roman Catholic Church; the Vatican stands alone in datelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Vatican' dateline separately and note institutional functions (pope, St. Peter's Basilica, Swiss Guard, etc.) when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vegetative state / comatose / non-responsive — people-first language
rubrics_metrics.description: Vegetative state is absence of responsiveness or consciousness; minimally conscious state has some awareness. Referring to a person as a 'vegetable' is offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise medical terminology or terms like 'comatose' or 'non-responsive.' If using 'vegetative state', use people-first phrasing ('a person in a vegetative state'). Avoid dehumanizing shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veiling — religious and cultural context
rubrics_metrics.description: Veiling is a religious practice (hijab) related to Islam but not specifically Arab; practices vary by region, class and personal choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid blanket judgments (liberating vs. oppressive); explain variability and do not assume uniform practice within families or communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Victim / suffering from / afflicted with / stricken with — avoid assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t assume how someone with a mental illness or condition is handling their life; prefer value-neutral, precise language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not preferred: 'She suffers from anxiety.' Preferred: 'She’s being treated for an anxiety disorder' or 'She is diagnosed with an anxiety disorder.' Use people-first language and avoid defining people by conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Victim vs. survivor — nuanced choice and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: There is debate over 'victim' vs 'survivor', especially in sexual assault/domestic violence contexts; each term carries implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask sources which term they prefer. Provide alternative phrasing (e.g., 'a person who was subjected to sexual violence', 'a person who was sexually assaulted', 'a person who survived sexual abuse', 'complainant' in court cases) to avoid limiting identity to the experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vietnamese names — name order
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically family name first, personal name last; in the U.S. Western order is common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On second reference, the personal name is sometimes used; be sensitive to preferred ordering and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vodou / Voodoo — spelling and sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Vodou (capitalized) is the acceptable spelling in academic and Haitian contexts; 'voodoo' may be offensive when used generically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid phrases like 'voodoo economics' except in direct quotes; acknowledge variations (Vodun, Voodoo) and cultural roots in West Africa and Caribbean syncretism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting Rights Act — historical summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Enacted Aug. 6, 1965 to oversee voter registration and elections in jurisdictions with discriminatory tests or low registration; banned literacy tests and expanded language access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note extensions (1970, 1975, 1982) and wide effects on voter registration and election of Black lawmakers; provide historical statistics when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Walking distance / walkability — accessibility caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms used in real estate and urban planning that may exclude people who use wheelchairs or have mobility disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'accessible' or 'pedestrian friendly' to be inclusive of people who use wheelchairs; treat people who use wheelchairs as pedestrians when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: West Indies — geographic definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Group of islands in the Caribbean Sea including Bahamas, Cuba, Jamaica, Haiti, Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico, U.S. Virgin Islands, Leeward and Windward Islands, Guyana, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain etymology (misnomer from Spanish explorers) and list constituent areas when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wheelchair / wheelchair-bound / confined to a wheelchair — people-first language
rubrics_metrics.description: People who use wheelchairs consider equipment part of personal space; 'wheelchair-bound' or 'confined to a wheelchair' are misleading and dehumanizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe someone as 'a person who uses a wheelchair' and explain why equipment is required when relevant. Avoid implying permanence or limitation; note mobility variances and activities beyond wheelchairs (sleep, transfer, drive).

rubrics_metrics.name: White flight — avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: White flight describes migration of White people from diversifying areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using the term; use precise demographic or sociological descriptions instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: White privilege — definition and framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantages for people with white skin that may be unrecognized and stem from systemic racism; can be economic, social or educational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain examples (freedom from barriers or suspicions), tie to institutional and systemic racism and use precise framing when reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: White — U.S. Census definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Census: 'a person having origins in any of the original peoples of Europe, the Middle East, or North Africa.' Categories reflect social definitions, not biological ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note 1997 OMB standards and the social/sociocultural nature of racial categories; avoid treating them as biological definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: White (capitalization debate) — usage guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: There has been debate about capitalizing 'White' analogous to capitalization of 'Black.' Most media organizations capitalized Black after 2020; many continue to lowercase White though some do capitalize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should be aware of newsroom policy variation (AP lowercases White; NABJ recommends capitalization of both). Monitor evolving usage and be consistent with your publication's policy.
